books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, “Spot Resolutions” in the House of Representatives, December 22, 1847. Public domain.
stimulus.text:
And whereas this House is desirous to obtain a full knowledge of all the facts which go to establish whether the particular spot on which the blood of our citizens was so shed was or was not at that time our own soil:

First. Whether the spot on which the blood of our citizens was shed, as in his message declared, was or was not within the territory of Spain, at least after the treaty of 1819, until the Mexican revolution.

Third. Whether that spot is or is not within a settlement of people, which settlement has existed ever since long before the Texas revolution, and until its inhabitants fled before the approach of the United States army.

Seventh. Whether our citizens, whose blood was shed, as in his message declared, were or were not, at that time, armed officers and soldiers, sent into that settlement by the military order of the President, through the Secretary of War.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Lincoln's resolutions best illustrate which of the following about opposition to the Mexican War?

options.text: Opposition came only from Southern Democrats who wanted more Mexican land annexed.
options.misconception: Southern Democrats mostly backed the war; the loudest opposition came from Northern Whigs like Lincoln.

options.text: Opponents of the war agreed that the United States should keep all of Mexico.
options.misconception: Few opponents wanted more land; many, like Lincoln, questioned taking any of it by war.

options.text: Congress passed Lincoln's resolutions and forced Polk to withdraw the army.
options.misconception: The House never acted on the resolutions, and the war ran on to the capture of Mexico City.

options.text: Northern Whigs challenged the war's justification by questioning Polk's account of how it began.

rationales.A: Southern Democrats backed Polk's war; the opposition sat with Northern Whigs and antislavery Northerners.
rationales.B: Lincoln and other critics wanted less conquest, not the annexation of all Mexico.
rationales.C: The resolutions were read and laid aside; Congress never forced Polk to answer them.
rationales.D: Lincoln, a freshman Whig from Illinois, attacked the war by demanding proof of Polk's claim that Mexico had invaded American soil.
rationales.general:
1. Place Lincoln in his party. He was a young Illinois Whig, and Whigs almost all opposed Polk's war.
2. See what he attacks. He does not argue about strategy; he attacks the story that justified the war.
3. Note the result. The House ignored the resolutions, but the challenge stuck to Lincoln as “spotty Lincoln.”
Remember: wartime dissent often takes the form of a question about the first blow — and the question can outlive the war.
